prompt: AKATA under the PIA prints hcdt 0.00 in 2029, 720000.00 in 2030 and 741600.00 in 2031, with opex 24000000.00, 24720000.00 and 25461600.00 in those years. Which opex is each levy computed on?

The current year's, but the levy is paid a year in arrears, so the 720000.00 charged on 2029's opex appears in the 2030 row as cash rather than as a liability.
The prior year's. pia_prior_year_opex_usd is 0, so 2029 pays none; 2030 reads 3 percent of 2029's 24000000.00 and 2031 reads 2030's 24720000.00.
A fixed sum that the engine escalates at the opex escalator, which is why the levy grows by the same 3 percent a year as the opex does.

prompt: The worked example prints nddc 15000000.00 on opex of 182500000.00 while pia_onshore_new_lease prints 2400000.00 on opex of 30000000.00 and capex of 50000000.00. Both carry the 3 percent rate. What makes the first one so large?
options: pia_nddc_levy_fixed_usd 15000000 is set on the worked example, and a fixed sum replaces the percentage whatever the opex is.
The worked example reads the levy on the prior year's opex of 170000000, and 3 percent of that is 5100000.00, which the engine then grosses up for the deductible NDDC.
The worked example is shallow water and the NDDC is charged on shallow water opex at a higher rate than the 3 percent that applies onshore.
The worked example's opex is uploaded as twelve monthly rows and the levy is charged on each row at 3 percent and then summed twelve times over.
explanation: Without a fixed sum the levy is 3 percent of the year's total annual budget, opex plus capex: 3 percent of 80000000.00 is 2400000.00. The fixed sum is a flat 15000000.00 in every year regardless of spend. On AKATA, with no fixed sum, the NDDC reads 7020000.00, 2091600.00 and 763848.00 in 2029 to 2031 beside HCDT of 0.00, 720000.00 and 741600.00. The prior-year opex feeds HCDT only, the terrain sets no NDDC rate, and monthly rows are summed to a year before any levy.

prompt: pia_prior_year_opex_zero removes the 5100000.00 HCDT from the worked example. Both tax bases rise by exactly 5100000.00, HCT rises from 285784994.46 to 287314994.46, and NPV rises from 141236909.83 to 143123909.83, less than the levy saved. Why less?
options: The NPV is on the real basis, and the 5100000.00 saved in 2025 money is deflated by the 3 percent inflation before it reaches the NPV.
The levy is deductible from both bases, so removing it raises HCT, CIT and TET, and the extra taxes take back part of the 5100000.00.
The levy is only partly removed: the engine keeps a minimum HCDT on the current year's opex when the prior year is zero, and that minimum still costs cash.
The 5100000.00 comes back as a deferred CPR cost, which the cap defers to a later year that the one-year field does not have.
explanation: Removing the levy raised both bases by the levy, so HCT, CIT and TET all rose and took back part of the saving. The two assessable profits stay equal to each other, 1058241648.19 with the levy and 1063341648.19 without it, because this oil-only field deducts HCDT and NDDC in both. The one-year field has no deflation to apply in its base year, HCDT has no minimum on the current year's opex, and the cost price ratio cap does not reach the levies.

prompt: On the worked example cit_assessable_profit and hct_assessable_profit both read 1058241648.19, and the NDDC is a fixed 15000000.00. Where does that NDDC sit?
options: Only in the HCT base; CIT takes the production allowance of 45625000.00 at the assessable stage in its place, and the two figures agree by coincidence of the round inputs.
In neither base: the HCDT of 5100000.00 and the TET of 31747249.45 are deducted there, and the NDDC comes off the cash alone, beside the taxes.
Only in the CIT base, with HCT deducting one year of capital allowance on the 300000000.00 of capex at the assessable stage to make up the difference.
In both bases: the hydrocarbon tax deducts it (PIA s.263(1)(f), (h)) as CIT does, so the two assessable profits agree.
explanation: Both profit taxes deduct HCDT and NDDC, and on an oil-only field the shared costs enter the hydrocarbon tax whole, so the two assessable profits are equal. The allowances come off later: 1058241648.19 less 60000000.00 of capital allowance less 45625000.00 of production allowance is hct_chargeable_profit 952616648.19, while CIT takes the capital allowance only, for cit_chargeable_profit 998241648.19. The production allowance never reaches CIT, TET is a tax and is deducted from neither base, and no capital allowance enters either assessable profit.

The cap is a share of revenue and never of the costs, it acts on converted and new leases alike, and on the worked example there is no pool and no binding cap in the only year.

prompt: cpr_forfeiture has a cpr_cap of 52000000.00, claims 52000000.00 and defers 8000000.00; the same row also carries a separate HCT loss of 512786.40 in hct_loss_carryforward. The field has no later year. What is the 8000000.00?
options: A tax loss carried forward at the HCT rate, which the engine reports in cpr_deferred_to_next rather than in the loss column because it arose from the cap.
A capital allowance the engine will claim in the next recovery year of the five, since the cap defers the allowance and not the opex.
A deferred cost that is not a tax loss and does not survive cessation; the KPI block reports CPR forfeited at cessation 8000000.00.
A cost that earns interest at the discount rate while it waits, so that the 8000000.00 grows to a larger claim in whichever year the cap next allows it.
explanation: pia_cpr_carry_two_years, at its stated 30 percent limit, adds 22000000.00 to the deferred pool in every year and forfeits 66000000.00 at cessation while hct_loss_carryforward reads 0.00 on every row; a deferral is not a loss. The 512786.40 on cpr_forfeiture is a real HCT loss: the production allowance takes the chargeable profit below zero after the capped claim. The deferral earns no interest and does not wait for the next allowance year.

prompt: AKATA at a CPR limit of 65 percent defers 1356394.56 in 2032 and 14120774.92 in 2033, then clears in 2034. At a limit of 40 percent HCT rises from 91654840.32 to 121989085.43 and NPV falls from 59766796.57 to 37056190.44. Why does a tighter cap hurt a declining field so much?
options: A tighter cap lengthens the capex recovery from five years to more, and the allowance that is pushed past 2035 is never claimed.
The cap is a share of a shrinking revenue while the costs are not shrinking, so more is deferred each year and what is still deferred when the field stops is lost.
The cap at 40 percent is read on the costs rather than on the revenue, and 40 percent of the costs is far less than 65 percent of them.
The deferred costs become tax losses, and losses under the PIA are relieved at a lower rate than the 30 percent HCT that the costs would have offset in the year they arose.
explanation: At 40 percent the deferral starts in 2030 and grows in every later year, and more than 101 million is still deferred when the field stops, so it is never claimed. At 65 percent in 2032 the cap is 73531102.32; in 2034 it is 54139706.27 against a claim of 49828572.67. CIT stays 102166298.31 at either limit because the cap limits the hydrocarbon tax only. The cap does not lengthen the five-year allowance, is read on revenue, and never turns a deferral into a loss.

At five years the worked example claims 242500000.00 against the cap. The CPR limit is a separate input, the ledger length does not decide the recovery life, and the restriction never causes a refusal.
